segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Now the first covenant had regulations for worship and the earthly holy place.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: For a tent was set up, the first one, in which were the lampstand and the table and the presentation of the loaves; this is called the Holy Place.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Behind the second curtain was a tent called the Holy of Holies,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: which had a golden altar of incense and the ark of the covenant, covered on all sides with gold. In the ark were a golden jar holding the manna, Aaron’s staff that had budded, and the tablets of the covenant,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: and above it were the cherubim of glory overshadowing the place of atonement. Of these things it is not possible to speak now in detail.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: With these things set up in this way, the priests go continually into the first tent, carrying out the acts of worship,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: but into the second only the high priest goes, once a year, and not without blood, which he offers for himself and for the sins the people have committed in ignorance.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: By this the Holy Spirit shows that the way into the holy place has not yet been revealed as long as the first tent still stands.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: This is a symbol for the present time, in accordance with which gifts and sacrifices are offered that cannot make the worshipper perfect in conscience,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: but deal only with foods and drinks and various washings, regulations for the flesh imposed until the time for setting things straight.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: But when Christ arrived as high priest of the good things that have come, then through the greater and more perfect tent, not made by hands, that is, not of this creation,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: and not through the blood of goats and calves but through his own blood, he entered the holy place once for all, obtaining eternal redemption.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: For if the blood of goats and bulls and the ashes of a heifer, sprinkled on those who have been defiled, make them holy so that their flesh is clean,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: how much more will the blood of Christ, who through the eternal Spirit offered himself without blemish to God, cleanse our conscience from dead works so that we may worship the living God!

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And for this reason he is the mediator of a new covenant, so that, a death having taken place for redemption from the transgressions committed under the first covenant, those who have been called may receive the promise of the eternal inheritance.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: For where there is a will, the death of the one who made it has to be established;

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: for a will takes effect only at death, since it is never in force while the one who made it is alive.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: That is why not even the first covenant was inaugurated without blood.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: For when every commandment had been spoken by Moses to all the people according to the law, he took the blood of the calves, with water and scarlet wool and hyssop, and sprinkled both the scroll itself and all the people,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: saying,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “This is the blood of the covenant that God has commanded for you.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And in the same way he sprinkled with the blood both the tent and all the vessels used in the service.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Indeed, according to the law almost everything is cleansed with blood, and without the shedding of blood there is no forgiveness.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: It was necessary, then, for the copies of the things in the heavens to be cleansed by these means, but the heavenly things themselves by better sacrifices than these.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: For Christ did not enter a holy place made by hands, a counterpart of the true one, but heaven itself, to appear now before the face of God on our behalf.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Nor did he enter to offer himself many times, as the high priest enters the holy place year after year with blood not his own;

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: otherwise he would have had to suffer many times since the foundation of the world. But as it is, he has been revealed once, at the end of the ages, to do away with sin through his sacrifice.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And just as it is appointed for people to die once, and after that comes judgment,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: so also Christ, having been offered once to bear the sins of many, will appear a second time, not to deal with sin, but to bring salvation to those who are eagerly waiting for him.

notes.note: The register's rendering for this word is 'righteous requirement', which suits Paul's usage. Here and in verse 10 the word has its common Septuagint sense of a statute or ordinance, namely the rules governing Israel's worship, and the author calls them 'regulations for the flesh' that were only temporary. 'Righteous requirements' would give them a moral weight the argument does not intend, so the usual 'regulations' is kept. The word 'covenant' is supplied in this verse, as in most translations; the Greek says only 'the first'.

The Greek word is the ordinary one for a tent, and it is the Septuagint's term for Israel's wilderness sanctuary. 'Tabernacle' comes from the Latin for the same thing but now sounds like a special religious object. The author uses 'tent' both for the whole structure and for each of its two rooms, and his argument turns on that. Several modern translations also use 'tent'.

notes.traditional: the showbread; the bread of the Presence
notes.note: The Greek phrase means the setting out of the loaves. It refers to the twelve loaves placed on the table before God each sabbath (Leviticus 24:5–9). 'Bread of the Presence' renders the Hebrew name; the Greek expression used here is different and is translated as it stands.

notes.traditional: golden altar of incense (older versions: golden censer)
notes.note: The word can mean either a censer or an incense altar. Most scholars take it as the altar, as Jewish writers of the period used the word. Exodus places that altar in the outer room, just in front of the curtain. The author may be linking it to the inner room because of its use on the Day of Atonement, but the matter is debated.

In the Septuagint this word names the gold cover of the ark, where blood was sprinkled on the Day of Atonement (Leviticus 16). 'Mercy seat' goes back to Tyndale and Luther and suggests a chair, which it was not. The same phrase is used for this word in Romans 3:25 so that the reader can see the connection, though the meaning there is disputed.
As in verse 1, the word means a ritual ordinance, not a 'righteous requirement' in the moral sense. The author is stressing that these rules concerned the body only and were temporary.

notes.phrase: the good things that have come
notes.note: Manuscripts are divided between 'the good things that have come' and 'the good things that are about to come'. The reading translated here has early and diverse support and is adopted by most modern editions. The other may have arisen under the influence of the similar phrase in 10:1.

Numbers 19 prescribes that a red heifer be burned and its ashes mixed with water. The mixture was sprinkled on anyone made ritually unclean by contact with a corpse. The uncleanness in view is ceremonial, a bar to taking part in worship; it is not moral guilt.

The Greek has no article: 'through eternal spirit'. Most interpreters take it as the Holy Spirit. Others understand Christ's own spirit or his eternal nature, in contrast to animal offerings that perish. A few manuscripts read 'Holy Spirit', which shows how early readers understood it.

The verb is the one used throughout the chapter for the service of God in the sanctuary (verses 1, 6, 9). Most translations switch to 'serve' here. 'Worship' is kept so that the contrast shows: the old rites could not perfect the worshipper, but Christ's blood fits people for the worship of the living God.

The Greek word translated 'covenant' everywhere else in this chapter was also the everyday term for a last will and testament. Most translators think the author plays on that second sense in verses 16–17, prompted by 'inheritance' in verse 15, and that is followed here. A minority of scholars keep 'covenant' throughout and read these verses as referring to the death, represented by sacrificed animals, that ratified a covenant. English cannot reproduce the single word.

notes.traditional: the heavenly things; the things in heaven
notes.note: The Greek is plural here, a Semitic way of speaking of God's dwelling, and the plural is kept. In verse 24 the word is singular and is translated 'heaven itself'. Most translations make no distinction.

notes.traditional: without sin; apart from sin; not to bear sin
notes.note: The Greek is literally 'apart from sin'. The contrast with the first appearing 'to bear the sins of many' (an echo of Isaiah 53:12) shows the sense: the second coming has nothing more to do with sin, which was dealt with once for all. The phrase does not mean Christ will then be sinless as though he had not been before.

candidates.reason: Recurs across the Gospels, Paul and Hebrews, and the covenant/will/testament choice at Hebrews 9:16–17 and Galatians 3:15–17 needs one policy.
Translations vary between 'serve' and 'worship' for this verb and for λατρεία, which hides the cultic sense and the links within Hebrews, Romans and Revelation.
A key term in Hebrews, also in John, Paul and James, where 'perfect', 'complete' and 'bring to its goal' compete and inconsistency would hide the theme.
'Tabernacle', 'tent', 'dwelling' and 'shelter' are used variously in the Gospels, Acts, Hebrews and Revelation for the same word, obscuring the wilderness-sanctuary allusion.
The word means both 'release' and 'forgiveness' (e.g. Luke 4:18 versus Matthew 26:28), and a consistent policy on when to use each is needed.
